summary: Kole Jain walks through designing a macOS app so it feels native, using a design-inspiration saving app as the worked example. He starts outside the main window: the app should be a system that appears where you need it (a shortcut-triggered quick-save window, popovers, toasts) and then gets out of the way, rather than a destination. For the main window he follows Apple's utility-app layout (top bar for global actions, sidebar for navigation, content in the centre), keeps the top of the window clear for dragging, drops the sidebar when navigation is simple, and uses empty states and progressive disclosure so the content can shine. He then covers designing light and dark mode separately instead of inverting, a floating search bar, visible feedback for every keyboard shortcut, drag and drop in and out of the app, a floating action bar, and onboarding that teaches shortcuts. For a design system this gives desktop-specific layout conventions, a dark-mode stance and a set of interaction patterns for utility apps.
key_ideas: A native-feeling Mac app is a system that shows up exactly where you need it, not a destination you have to visit.
To design like Apple, first get comfortable with the UI that lives outside the main window (popovers, new windows, notifications, shortcut-triggered panels).
Think about how the user actually works (hopping between Figma, code and Notion) and give them a keyboard shortcut to act without switching context.
An app holds the user's own content that they add and change, so it is more user-focused than a landing page, even when the components look similar.
Apple's utility apps share one layout: global actions on top, navigation in a sidebar, content in the centre, with the traffic lights treated like any other element.
The top of a Mac window is used for dragging the window, so keep it uncluttered.
Skip the sidebar when navigation is just browsing and searching, so the UI becomes a container for the user's content.
Use empty states and progressive disclosure: show only what the user needs in that moment and hide filters until there is content to filter.
Before adding colors or effects, find the minimum UI that lets the content shine.
Light and dark mode are not exact opposites; they should feel different but consistent.
Search should be prominent and accessible; a floating search bar with a slide-out preview keeps a one-screen app on one screen.
Every keyboard shortcut needs visible feedback, a micro-animation or at least a state change, or users assume something went wrong.
Drag and drop should work both into the app and out of it to other apps.
Optimistic UI means processing a save in the background while assuming it will succeed, as Apple Mail does when moving email to trash.
Even desktop apps benefit from onboarding, especially to teach keyboard shortcuts, which are powerful but easy to forget.

topics.name: Desktop and macOS apps
topics.summary: The whole video: native macOS patterns such as shortcut-triggered windows, the top-bar/sidebar/content layout, the window drag area, traffic lights, search, drag and drop and the share button.

topics.name: Navigation and sidebars
topics.summary: Apple utility apps put navigation in a sidebar; the example app skips it because navigation is only browsing and searching, which frees room for large images.

topics.name: Spacing and layout
topics.summary: Top for global actions, sidebar for navigation, content in the centre; keep roughly the top 50 pixels clear because it is used to drag the window.

topics.name: Dark mode and themes
topics.summary: Respect the system light/dark setting; do not directly invert colors, because dark mode needs more separation between colors than light mode. Light and dark should feel different but consistent.

topics.name: Feedback, empty and loading states
topics.summary: A simple empty state invites the first action; optimistic UI shows a save as done straight away; every shortcut needs a visible state change.

topics.name: Micro-interactions
topics.summary: The quick-save panel slides in on Command Shift S, slides away on Escape and turns into a toast on Enter; the collapsed search bar expands when clicked or triggered.

topics.name: Toasts and notifications
topics.summary: After saving, the quick-save window collapses into a toast notification and slides off the screen.

topics.name: Gestures and drag
topics.summary: Drag and drop of anything anywhere is a must: drop content into the quick-save window and drag content out to Figma, Finder or elsewhere.

topics.name: Modals and popovers
topics.summary: Popovers and new windows are part of feeling native; onboarding is a modal, and a settings popover holds the shortcut cheat sheet, panel side and light/dark setting.

topics.name: Buttons and actions
topics.summary: Buttons in the quick-save window show keyboard shortcut reminders; a floating action bar in the preview gives copy, find and delete; Apple's universal share button is common.

topics.name: Onboarding
topics.summary: Desktop apps should not skip onboarding; the example uses a simple modal with micro-interactions that closes when the user performs the shortcut, and a shortcut cheat sheet.

topics.name: Design process
topics.summary: Start with how the user will actually interact and the UI outside the main window, then the main window, and ask what minimum UI lets the content shine before adding color or effects.

quotes: the app shouldn't be a destination, but a system exactly where you need it.
Design light and dark mode not as exact opposites.
If you don't see a change, you assume that something went wrong.

rules.rule: Design the app to appear where the user needs it (for example a window opened by a keyboard shortcut) and then get out of the way, instead of making it a destination they must visit.
rules.why: To feel native, an app should be a system exactly where you need it, like Spotlight and Raycast.
rules.evidence: To feel native, the app shouldn't be a destination

rules.rule: Keep quick-capture windows minimal: drop the traffic lights and include only a drop area, a simple input and a few buttons.
rules.why: The window should stay out of the way and be as minimal as possible, like widgets that slide in quietly from the side.
rules.evidence: toss the traffic lights and just add the basics of a drop area

rules.rule: Show keyboard shortcut reminders on the buttons they trigger.
rules.why: Shortcuts are powerful but easy to forget, so users need reminders [inferred].
rules.evidence: I'll add in some keyboard shortcut reminders to those

rules.rule: Use optimistic UI for background saves: show the action as done immediately (for example collapse into a toast) while processing continues in the background.
rules.why: The image is processed and saved in the background while the UI assumes it will succeed; Apple Mail does the same when moving email to trash.
rules.evidence: These are also all good examples of optimistic UI

rules.rule: In a utility app, put global actions in the top bar, navigation in a sidebar and the main content in the centre.
rules.why: Almost all of Apple's utility apps (Finder, Notes, Reminders, Calendar, Settings) use this layout because apps are user-focused.
rules.evidence: the top for global level actions, the sidebar for navigation, and the main content in the center

rules.rule: Integrate the traffic light window buttons into the top bar or sidebar and treat them like any other element.
rules.why: Apple's own apps do this seamlessly.
rules.evidence: seamlessly integrate the traffic light actions into the UI

rules.rule: Do not clutter the top of a macOS window with actions; roughly the top 50 pixels is the window drag area, so let it breathe.
rules.why: That area is used to drag the window.
rules.evidence: the top roughly 50 pixels of their apps allow window dragging

rules.rule: Skip the sidebar when navigation is only browsing and searching, and use the space for the user's content.
rules.why: It gives extra room for large images and lets the UI act as a container for the user's content.
rules.evidence: we can skip the sidebar entirely

rules.rule: Show a simple empty state that invites the first action, and hide filters and other components until the user has content.
rules.why: Progressive disclosure: only show what the user needs in that moment; filters aren't useful until there is content.
rules.evidence: This is a form of progressive disclosure

rules.rule: Show an item's full data only when the user clicks on it.
rules.why: Another form of progressive disclosure that keeps the browsing view focused on content.
rules.evidence: only showing all of the data when the user actually clicks on the image

rules.rule: Before adding colors or effects, decide the minimum UI needed to let the content shine.
rules.why: The UI of a content app is a container for the user's content and should stay out of the way.
rules.evidence: What is the minimum UI needed to really let that content shine?

rules.rule: Respect the system light and dark mode setting as much as possible.
rules.why: All Macs let users switch between light and dark mode.
rules.evidence: those settings should be respected as much as possible

rules.rule: Do not create one mode by directly inverting the other's colors; design light and dark mode as different but consistent.
rules.why: Dark mode needs colors that are more different from each other than light mode; directly inverting into light mode makes the contrast much higher and doesn't look stellar, while collapsing the colors to be more similar looks a lot more refined.
rules.evidence: Design light and dark mode not as exact opposites

rules.rule: Make search prominent and always accessible.
rules.why: Every native Mac app (Music, Shortcuts, Weather) has search that is prominent and accessible.
rules.evidence: everything has search, and it's always prominent and accessible

rules.rule: When search results look like the browse view, show the result count and a clear (X) button in the search bar, and the query with a back arrow in the top left.
rules.why: The browsing and search pages look quite similar.
rules.evidence: we'll add the search results count to the search bar and an X to clear

rules.rule: Give every keyboard shortcut, and every interaction, immediate visible feedback: a micro-animation or at least a state change.
rules.why: If users don't see a change, they assume something went wrong.
rules.evidence: micro animations, or at least a state change, are instrumental

rules.rule: Collapse a tool such as the floating search bar until the user needs it, and expand it to full size when it is clicked or its shortcut is triggered.
rules.why: It stays out of the way until the user needs it while still giving immediate feedback.
rules.evidence: we'll collapse it down. and clicking or triggering the shortcut beautifully expands it

rules.rule: Support drag and drop both into the app and out of it to other apps (for example into Figma or Finder).
rules.why: It makes the experience feel effortless; Apple does this across Photos, Finder, Reminders and Shortcuts.
rules.evidence: drag and drop of anything anywhere is a must

rules.rule: Put frequent item actions (copy, find, delete) in a floating action bar in the preview panel.
rules.why: Keeps common actions easy to access so they feel natural rather than like features.
rules.evidence: we'll also have a floating action bar in the preview slide out

rules.rule: Include onboarding in desktop apps and use it to teach keyboard shortcuts, and provide a shortcut cheat sheet (for example in a settings popover).
rules.why: Keyboard shortcuts are very powerful but easy to forget.
rules.evidence: It's important to educate the users on keyboard shortcuts

rules.rule: Before designing screens, work out how and where the user will actually interact with the product, for example while they are working in other apps.
rules.why: To feel native the app should be a system exactly where you need it, so how the user will actually interact with the final product is super important.
rules.evidence: thinking about how the user will actually interact with a final product is super important

rules.rule: Design an app around the user's own content that they add and change, not like a landing page of pre-generated content, even when the components look similar.
rules.why: A landing page is pre-generated content that doesn't really change, while an app holds the user's information, so apps are much more user-focused; the source calls this crucial.
rules.evidence: an app is meant to hold the user's information

rules.rule: Keep a utility app simple and good at doing one thing, so its UI can stay hyperfocused.
rules.why: Apple's utility apps (Finder, Notes, Reminders, Calendar, Settings) are wonderfully simple and good at doing one thing, so the UI can stay hyperfocused.
rules.evidence: wonderfully simple and good at doing one thing

rules.rule: Give a floating quick-capture window a native blur, as Paste does.
rules.why: The source copies Paste's native blur for its quick-save window, following apps that integrate seamlessly like native windows; it gives no other reason.
rules.evidence: kind of like how paste has a native blur

rules.rule: Let search match what is actually in the content (for example image recognition on images), not just titles.
rules.why: A query such as 'mobile app with houses and a calendar' then returns relevant results.
rules.evidence: search based on what's actually in the image instead of just by titles

rules.rule: Offer Apple's universal share button on items alongside the app's own actions.
rules.why: You'll find it on almost all Apple apps because sometimes it is just more convenient.
rules.evidence: Apple's universal share button because sometimes that is just more convenient

decisions.question: Should the app be a place people go to, or something that appears where they already are?

options.name: Destination app
options.effect: Users must switch to the app's main window to act, breaking their flow [inferred].
options.when: Not recommended for utility apps in this source [inferred].

options.name: System that appears when needed
options.effect: A shortcut-triggered window, popover or panel appears over whatever the user is doing and then gets out of the way, like Spotlight, Raycast or Paste.
options.when: When users find or capture things while doing other work, such as moving between Figma, code and Notion.

decisions.recommendation: Be a system exactly where you need it: a shortcut opens a minimal quick-save window, because that is what makes a Mac app feel native.
decisions.evidence: the app shouldn't be a destination, but a system

decisions.question: Does the main window need a sidebar?

options.name: Apple utility layout with sidebar
options.effect: Top bar for global actions, sidebar for navigation, content in the centre, as in Finder, Notes, Reminders, Calendar and Settings.
options.when: When the app has real navigation between sections [inferred].

options.name: No sidebar
options.effect: More room for large content such as images; the UI becomes a container for the user's content.
options.when: When navigation is really just browsing and searching.

decisions.recommendation: Skip the sidebar for the example app because its navigation is only browsing and searching, which lets it stay out of the way.
decisions.evidence: we can skip the sidebar entirely

decisions.question: How should light and dark mode colors relate to each other?

options.name: Direct inversion
options.effect: Contrast becomes much higher and it doesn't look stellar.

options.name: Designed separately but consistent
options.effect: Dark mode colors spread further apart; light mode colors collapsed to be more similar, which looks more refined.

decisions.recommendation: Design light and dark mode not as exact opposites; they should feel different but consistent, because dark mode needs more separation between colors.
decisions.evidence: Design light and dark mode not as exact opposites

decisions.question: How should search work in a mostly one-screen app?

options.name: Command palette or universal search
options.effect: Sleek and intuitive, but most items take you to an entirely new screen.
options.when: Powerful software such as Notion, Obsidian or Attio.

options.name: Floating search bar with a slide-out preview
options.effect: Search happens in place; results stay on the same screen and a preview slides out from the side.
options.when: When the goal is to remain largely a one-screen application, like most of Apple's utilities.

decisions.recommendation: The source chose the floating search bar and slide-out preview to keep the app on one screen.
decisions.evidence: I opted for a floating search bar and a slide out preview instead

decisions.question: How should a desktop app onboard new users?

options.name: No onboarding
options.effect: Typical of Apple's own apps; shortcuts may go undiscovered [inferred].

options.name: Rich onboarding process
options.effect: A fuller guided flow, like Raycast's.
options.when: When the app has a lot to teach [inferred].

options.name: Simple modal with micro-interactions
options.effect: A modal that closes when the user performs the key shortcut, which makes the quick-save window pop out.
options.when: When the main thing to learn is a shortcut.

decisions.recommendation: Use a simple onboarding modal that teaches the shortcut by having the user perform it, because shortcuts are powerful but easy to forget.
decisions.evidence: The way to close it is to execute the shortcut

decisions.question: Should the app follow the system light and dark mode setting?

options.name: Light and dark, following the system setting
options.effect: The app matches the light or dark mode the person chose for their Mac.
options.when: By default: the source says those settings should be respected as much as possible.

options.name: Plus a light/dark setting in the app
options.effect: The settings popover holds the light and dark mode settings next to the shortcut cheat sheet and the quick-save panel side.
options.when: The source's example app includes it.

decisions.recommendation: Respect the system light/dark setting as much as possible, and put the light and dark mode settings in the app's settings popover.
decisions.evidence: those settings should be respected as much as possible

decisions.question: Should filters and item details be visible from the start, or revealed when needed?

options.name: Show everything up front
options.effect: Filters and full item data are on screen before they are useful [inferred].

options.name: Progressive disclosure
options.effect: A simple empty state first; filters and other components stay hidden until the user starts saving; an item's full data shows only when it is clicked.
options.when: When the UI is mainly a container for the user's content.

decisions.recommendation: Only show the user what they need to see in that moment: hide filters until there is content and show item data on click.
decisions.evidence: This is a form of progressive disclosure

process.detail: Get comfortable with the UI that lives outside the main window (popovers, new windows, notifications) and decide how the app appears where the user needs it.

process.step: Map how the user actually works
process.detail: Look at what the user is doing when they need the app (for example editing in Figma, then code, then Notion) and give them a keyboard shortcut to act without switching.
Keep it minimal: no traffic lights, a drop area, an input, a few buttons with shortcut reminders, and a native blur.
On Enter, collapse the window into a toast and slide it off screen, treating the save optimistically while it processes in the background.
Use top bar for global actions, sidebar for navigation and content in the centre, integrate the traffic lights, keep the top clear for dragging, and drop the sidebar if navigation is simple.

process.step: Design the empty state and progressive disclosure
process.detail: Show a simple empty state inviting the first action; hide filters until there is content; reveal item details on click. Ask what minimum UI lets the content shine.
Respect the system setting and design each mode separately rather than inverting, so they feel different but consistent.
Make search prominent; choose between a command palette and a floating search bar with slide-out preview; add result count, clear button, query label and back arrow.
Make every shortcut produce a micro-animation or state change, for example the panel sliding in on Command Shift S and away on Escape, and the collapsed search bar expanding.

process.step: Support drag and drop and quick actions
process.detail: Let content be dropped in and dragged out to other apps, add a floating action bar (copy, find, delete) and the share button.

process.step: Add onboarding and a shortcut cheat sheet
process.detail: Use a simple onboarding modal that teaches the key shortcut, and put a cheat sheet, the panel side and light/dark setting in a settings popover.

caveats: Sponsor segment: Matter by JetBrains, an AI development companion used to prototype the UI from a Figma link; its claims are a paid read, not design guidance.
Self-promotion: the app built in the video is offered for download and its waitlist (kolejain.com/stash) is linked in the description.
Published 2025-12-02; macOS conventions described are as of that date.
Opinion framing: Apple is presented as the pinnacle of design; the patterns are the presenter's recommendations, not Apple guidelines quoted.

The dark-mode passage is muddled in auto-captions ('Directly inverting the colors looks okay' then 'doesn't look stellar'); the reading that dark mode needs wider color separation and light mode colors should be collapsed closer is the most consistent interpretation [inferred].
Auto-caption fixes: 'commandshifts' is Command Shift S, 'poll request' is pull request [inferred], 'one-sreen' is one-screen, 'atio' is probably Attio [inferred].

The video is visual; most on-screen examples are described only by narration, and no concrete color, size, duration or easing values are given apart from the roughly 50-pixel drag area. No media list was available.
